title: Prompt-cache forensics from 30 real sessions: 68% of cache writes come from 36 events (TTL expiry, microcompact, resume) — with paper-backed mitigations
excerpt:
*Measured 13/09/2026 by one user: Windows 11, Claude desktop app, Claude Code 2.1.266, Opus 5 / Fable 5.1, 1M context enabled. Version numbers as reported by the app.*

## TL;DR

- Across 30 sessions (3,203 API calls), **cache reads are 64% of API-equivalent cost**, cache writes 28%, output 9%. Average context per call is **320k tokens** (median 239k, p90 707k). The system-prompt prefix is ~83k of that (49k shared across projects + ~34k project-specific); **the rest is conversation history**.
- **68% of all cache-write tokens (14.8M of 21.7M) come from 36 events**, not from steady-state growth. Three causes, all client-observable:
  1. **1h TTL expiry** — 19 events, 9.4M tokens. Expected, but each one re-writes 300–860k of history.
  2. **Mid-history pruning (microcompact)** — 4 events in one session, 3.0M tokens. Each time ~83k of old tool results were cleared, `cache_read` fell to the shared prefix (47,638) and 620–830k were re-written. Once it happened **two calls after** a TTL re-write: 1.3M tokens written inside one minute, where a prune aligned to the cold miss would have cost nothing extra.
  3. **Resume / model switch** — ~6 events, ~1.9M tokens. On resume `cache_read` equals the *shared* prefix only (49,043), so the project part of the system prompt is not byte-stable across sessions and the whole history is re-written behind it.
- The suggestions below are small and mostly scheduling: prune when the cache is already cold, prune in bigger batches, keep the project prefix byte-stable on resume, and consider a bounded-history default. Each has a paper behind it (section 4).
- A measurement pitfall worth documenting: **the session `.jsonl` writes one `assistant` line per content block (thinking / text / tool_use), each carrying the same `usage`.** Summing usage per line overstates everything ~1.7×. Dedup by `(message.id, requestId)`.

## 1. Method

- Source: `~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl`, the 30 most recently modified sessions (25 with ≥5 calls). Only `type == "assistant"` entries with `message.usage`.
- Dedup by `(message.id, requestId)` → 5,568 lines become 3,203 calls.
- "Cache break" = a call whose `cache_creation_input_tokens` exceeds 20% of the previous call's total context and 20k tokens. Classified by wall-clock gap to the previous call (>60 min → TTL), by whether the context shrank, and by what happened between the two calls (

title: [Feature Request] Unified user state across Cowork and Claude chat — shared memory, files, skills, connectors
excerpt:
## Problem

Claude Cowork (Desktop research preview) and Claude chat (web + iOS + Android) operate as siloed surfaces despite serving the same authenticated user:

- Cowork can read/write a scoped folder on my Mac, run skills, use plugins, and execute multi-step file-centric work — but only at my desk, with no mobile equivalent.
- Chat (especially the iOS app) is where I actually spend time when I'm away from my desk. It has its own memory, its own connectors, its own thread history.

When I shift surfaces during a workflow, context resets. Memory doesn't follow. Files I worked on in Cowork aren't visible in chat on the go. Connector state and authentications don't carry. Skills configured for one don't appear in the other (related: #20697).

## Use case

Typical day: morning at desk → Cowork on a project folder → commute → continue thinking in iOS chat → evening back at desk → Cowork to execute. Today this requires manual context-passing. I use Claude Code Dispatch from iOS to route specific tasks to a Claude Code session on my Mac, which works well, but it doesn't solve the underlying memory and file split — it just routes a single task across.

I've worked around this by making Obsidian Sync my canonical file backend (Claude Code reads it directly on Mac, Obsidian Sync handles mobile access), but that only partially closes the gap and doesn't address memory or connector state.

## Suggested approach

Treat Cowork and chat as two surfaces over a single unified user state:

1. **Shared memory** — claude.ai memory, Cowork auto-memory, and Claude Code CLAUDE.md should converge into one coherent layer the user can read/write from any surface.
2. **Shared file workspace** — when Cowork has a folder scoped, that folder (or selected artifacts) should be reachable from chat as a viewable/searchable resource. From iOS I should be able to ask "what's the latest on the X analysis I was working on in Cowork?" and get an answer grounded in Cowork's actual files.
3. **Shared skills and connectors** — already requested for skills in #20697; extend to connectors and authentication state.
4. **Surface handoff affordances** — explicit "continue this in Cowork" / "continue this in chat" actions, analogous to Claude Code's `/desktop` and `--teleport` for the coding case.

- #2511 — Claude Code ↔ Claude Projects

title: Expose rate-limit reset times, balance, plan as status_line tokens
excerpt:
## Summary

The CLI status_line exposes `five-hour-limit` and `weekly-limit` as percentages only. The underlying rate-limit data is richer — `account/rateLimits/read` returns `resetsAt`, `windowDurationMins`, `credits.balance`, `planType` — but those fields aren't reachable via status_line tokens.

## Missing tokens (as of 0.133.0)

1. `five-hour-limit-reset` — formatted local time of `primary.resetsAt`
2. `weekly-limit-reset` — formatted local time of `secondary.resetsAt`
3. `credits-balance` — `credits.balance` (e.g. `$766.76`) when `credits.hasCredits && !credits.unlimited`
4. `plan-type` — `planType` (e.g. `prolite`)
5. (optional) `rate-limit-window-primary` / `-secondary` — `windowDurationMins` formatted

## Use case

Mirrors Claude Code's statusline which shows percentage + reset time. Without reset times the bare percentage is hard to act on — "5h 80%" doesn't tell you whether you have 10 minutes or 3 hours of breathing room. With it:

```
... · 5h 80% @11:36pm · weekly 83% @5/27 5:40am · ...
```

## Workaround

Spawn `codex app-server` from outside, JSON-RPC handshake, call `account/rateLimits/read`, parse, render. Works but adds ~3-5s subprocess startup per query and requires users to build their own caching layer. The data is already there inside the running CLI; surfacing it as a token is a small change.

## Verified data shape (0.133.0)

`account/rateLimits/read` returns:

```json
{
  "rateLimits": {
    "limitId": "codex",
    "primary": { "usedPercent": 25, "windowDurationMins": 300, "resetsAt": 1779459394 },
    "secondary": { "usedPercent": 18, "windowDurationMins": 10080, "resetsAt": 1779826837 },
    "credits": { "hasCredits": true, "unlimited": false, "balance": "766.76..." },
    "planType": "prolite",
    "rateLimitReachedType": null
  },
  "rateLimitsByLimitId": { ... }
}
```

## Acceptance

Adding these to the existing config:

```toml
status_line = ["model-with-reasoning", "codex-version", "context-remaining",
               "five-hour-limit", "five-hour-limit-reset",
               "weekly-limit", "weekly-limit-reset",
               "credits-balance", "project", "git-branch"]
```

Produces:

```
gpt-5.5 high · 0.133.0 · Context 28% left · 5h 25% @11:36pm · weekly 18% @5/27 5:40am · $766.76 · self-service-workbench · main
```

Thanks for the great CLI.

Visible website permissions and stored global allow rules disagree with the chat-scoped denial. The user cannot complete authorized desktop/mobile QA of their website.

Diagnosis scope
The files confirm conflicting global and session permissions. This suggests precedence or invalidation behavior, but the exact application-level cause has not been established. No permission files were modified, no policy bypass attempted. No credentials, customer data, chat ID, or raw transcripts are included.

Request
Please document a supported session-denial reset or fix invalidation of stale per-chat origin decisions when the user explicitly changes website permissions.

title: [BUG] Headless chrome.exe launched by Claude Code on Windows triggers failed logons and locks IdP-managed accounts
excerpt:
## Summary

On Windows 11 devices managed by an identity provider (JumpCloud), each time Claude Code launches `chrome.exe` (or `msedge.exe`) in headless mode from the shell to convert local HTML into PDF/PNG, Windows records a burst of failed logon attempts attributed to the browser process. The identity provider counts them as wrong-password attempts and locks the user's account. No password is being typed; the only trigger is the headless browser launch.

## Environment

- Claude Code desktop app on Windows 11 Pro, devices bound to JumpCloud
- Users who ask Claude Code for PDFs/images rendered from HTML get locked out; users with the same software who never ask for that never do
- Does not reproduce on macOS with the same workflow

## Evidence

On one affected machine, 6 of 7 failed-login bursts over two days match, to the minute, a headless Chrome launch by a Claude Code session (screenshots of a local HTML deck, HTML to PDF, a script rendering images). Attempts inside a burst are 1.5 to 3 s apart and keep going after the account is already locked. JumpCloud's troubleshooting docs note that browser automation tools can trigger a Chromium defect that produces failed logins per session, which matches.

## Expected

Rendering a local HTML file with headless Chrome should not generate Windows credential validation attempts.

## Workaround applied

Global CLAUDE.md rule for Windows users: never invoke `chrome.exe`/`msedge.exe` headless to convert HTML; hand the HTML to the user or produce .docx/.pptx instead.

## Asks

1. Does the default HTML to PDF/PNG path on Windows launch headless Chrome with the user's default profile? A temporary `--user-data-dir` plus `--no-first-run --disable-sync` may avoid whatever triggers the credential check.
2. A built-in renderer or a documented safe set of flags for Windows would prevent silent lockouts on SSO-managed devices.

Happy to share Windows Security event 4625 details (LogonType/SubStatus) once collected.

title: Astation handoff: independent remote clients, staged approvals, rich chat
excerpt:
This is the latest Astation-to-Atem handoff for independent remote clients. Please review the joint contract decisions before implementing admission or emitting new signed push fields.

Sources:
- Astation draft PR #58: https://github.com/Agora-Build/Astation/pull/58
- Reviewed handoff snapshot: Astation commit a9e850a0a76e81b131697fe1ce8ee8fb076be108.
- Remote/API design: https://github.com/Agora-Build/Astation/blob/a9e850a0a76e81b131697fe1ce8ee8fb076be108/designs/protocol/remote-agent-api.md
- Signed push/scheduler proposal: https://github.com/Agora-Build/Astation/blob/a9e850a0a76e81b131697fe1ce8ee8fb076be108/designs/protocol/approval-push-proof.md
- Current readable copies (VPN): https://truck.netbird.cloud:58310/protocol/remote-agent-api.md and https://truck.netbird.cloud:58310/protocol/approval-push-proof.md

## Product requirements

1. Mobile/native Astation connects independently to the original Atem host, whether Mac Astation is online or offline. Mac and mobile can view the same original agent sessions concurrently. The Atem host itself must remain running/reachable. Each controller has its own enrolled keys and attachment; no dependency on the Mac's local API or borrowed credentials.
2. Keep r8 operation semantics: one terminal/control lease per agent session; prompt Send atomically acquires an unowned lease, and taking another holder requires confirmed expected-controller takeover. Approval answers and rule revocation are lease-free with control permission and the exact request/rule. Reading or approving on mobile must not disturb the Mac's lease. Reconnect never silently regains control.
3. Use WSS first. A later Agora Signaling adapter may improve end-user connectivity, but must preserve endpoint proof, encryption, ordering, target/lease fencing and durable receipts. Verify runtime/platform and network support before enabling it. Whole-message responses are sufficient; token-by-token streaming is not required.
4. Preserve rich response content. Existing text parts already carry Markdown; retain original source, typed tool/approval parts, IDs and ordering in live/history/API delivery. Mobile will render paragraphs, headings, bold/italic, highlighted links, lists, code blocks with highlighting/copy, and tables. Basic formatting needs no new host message type. Images/audio/PDF/files are separate capabilities and must not be implied by Markdown supp

title: Show HN: AWKLog – a minimalist Datalog interpreter in Awk
author: stass
content_excerpt:
For many of the projects I work on I found myself wanting to use a relational language like Datalog to generate C source from specifications, do verification during build or maintain a task database.

However pulling a full blown Souffle or SWI-PL as a build dependency is always a PITA and also an overkill.

So I (with the help of Claude) built awklog, a pure POSIX awk based interpreter. Copy it to your project and use during build stage or test stage with no extra dependencies.

It's a semi-naive interpreter, so decently fast, and certainly fast enough for anything you might need to do as a dev tool.

One cool usecase in particular I've been a heavy user of is a task system maintained directly in the project git repo. Just create a text file with tuples describing your tasks, their states, dependencies, hypotheses and so on. AWKLog will be able to query it for you, even recursively, and provide instant answers. Easy for AI agents to query too and no remote infrastructure dependencies at all. Everything stays in GIT, version controlled.

I hope other people will find this tool useful too.

title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
author: dataflow
content_excerpt:
> understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions

He phrases it like these criteria are requirements, but they really aren't for every problem. They make sense for those theoretical problems whose solutions' main values lie in their understandability and further development, but not every problem is like that. Some problems' solutions are just revolutionary on their own even if you contribute or understand absolutely nothing else. AI technology itself is an example of this!

To give a trivial hypothetical counterexample: if you came up with a solution for the traveling salesman problem that is both empirically sufficiently faster than the state of the art, that is an immense contribution and you absolutely deserve the credit for it regardless of whether you or anyone else understands how/why it works. It could literally even produce wrong results 50% of the time and still revolutionize humanity if it's efficient enough when it's correct. Denying them credit because they didn't understand the algorithm would be ludicrous - the results stand & speak for themselves.

Statisticians, traditional-AI researchers, etc. had to learn this the hard way when (basically black-box) neural nets became so good that their otherwise-elegant & explainable classical algorithms just stopped being able to compete in more and more applications, and got left behind. Are mathematicians looking to repeat that history?

title: AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System
author: bitwize
content_excerpt:
...For now.

Frontier models are generating sensible abstract engineering decisions for nontrivial code bases. Phase 1 (GPT 4 era) was "fancy autocomplete": it could generate a function or complete a clause before losing the plot. Phase 2 (Opus 4.x era) was the spec-driven development era, involving careful construction of guardrails and guidelines and steering the agents as they worked. Phase 3 is the beginning of the "software factory" era. You can now one-shot nontrivial apps with a prompt that leaves most of the specifics up to the agents. You just can't do this for like, a whole enterprise—maybe a microservice.

Another phase or two, and you can pretty much say goodbye to 95% of SWE jobs. The only people left involved in the software development process will be business analysts, product managers, and perhaps designers if they don't want the UI to look all "AI ass-ugly". A handful of trillion-dollar companies will retain a few really smart people who could code by hand if they wanted to, to keep the models trained and topped up on good practices. But line-of-business, which was the bread and butter for software engineers for going on 70 years now, will be done by machine. Humans will specify, and humans will QA the results, and that's it.

title: Ask HN: What are you working on? (November 2026)
author: srid68
content_excerpt:
1-year part-time experiment: can you build a large project with AI writing the code and AI plus deterministic tools verifying/guiding/enforcing it for structural and behavior consistency, without a human reading the code?

I'm building a polyglot web framework in 15 languages, with C# and Lean4 as the reference implementations. Structural and behavioral audits using deterministic tools check that every port stays consistent with the reference. It's about 1.8M lines now. I have not reviewed the code/neither have i verified the behavior tests except at the time of giving requirement and never seen some of the language code at all.

The question is how far can we produce "working code → correct code [Possible] → good code [Unknown]" with deterministic audits correcting structure, ai mistakes and behavior validation.

So far the quality looks acceptable with lots of correction of AI output done without looking, but it isn't fully verified.

Line counts per language, with changes since August: https://claude.ai/artifact/5f1m1pTM7tZ4boQzwsoAG7

author: minraws

As much as I would like to say I agree, I don't really like the LLM ui replacements. I absolutely hate them, they are just horrible, claude code itself is a horrible way of producing code/output you aren't seeing the logical pieces of your project you are largely stuck in a text box with a diff viewer and unable to parse what's happening.

Something like codex desktop is slightly better but still a horrible interface for developing software in any form of serious capacity.

Sure it works because the friction of manually working is just so damn high. And there aren't good alternatives, the jump from pi to claude to codex being almost negligible for most folks is a very high signal this entire pattern just doesn't really work.

I don't yet know where we will land or will we suffer with the current bad type text in a box ux for the next few years but I am certain this is not it.

I am still trying to work out what is it though, so well we will see when we get there.

Not using tools is a good example of the issue, you give up a lot of control to do that, sometimes it's good enough often it's not, and often it's worse because you don't even realize how much control you have given up.

I don't think we will do natural language interactions with our computers, I honestly feel like we will do something more intent based. If LLMs can know from our words what we want to do, then they can certain infer from what we are doing stuff we are about to do.

title: AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System
author: lnkdinsuxs
content_excerpt:
> It's going to enable me to do less software development and more marketing? Goodie, I'm so happy I could puke.

If you hate marketing, don't do it. If you enjoy software development, have fun doing it.

However, you will remain an employee and you have to appreciate the pros and cons of being an employee. The other thing you have to appreciate is that the number of employees writing code who are AI, are cheaper than any human on the planet and works 24x7 without complaining or asking for a raise is going to go up. Likely exponentially.

This doesn't mean demand for good software developers is going to go down, but increasingly, software development is likely going to look like how one human Amazon warehouse worker wears special harnesses that allow them to lift far more weight, walk longer distances and interact with dozens of robots in the warehouse.

As I said in the parent it's not for everyone but a lot more people who were struggling to start their own venture will now be more capable of and have more freedom.

It might very well turn out that in a few years, the only way to enjoy software development the way you like it, is to establish your own boutique software development company.

title: Show HN: Nonce – Open-source, least-privilege Gmail access for AI agents
author: richardmeng
content_excerpt:
Hi HN! We built nonce, an open-source tool that sits between personal AI agents (Muse, Grok, ChatGPT, Claude) and your personal data in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and more.

Today, if you connect Gmail to an AI agent like Muse, it can read your entire inbox. Whether on purpose or not, they can read far more emails than needed. This poses a huge data-privilege risk, in which personal data is accessed without limits.

With nonce, the AI will no longer hold your Google or Slack tokens. To read anything, it has to show its intent first:

User's question: When does my flight to Tokyo leave? Agent's justification: Need the airline confirmation email Agent's search query: from:united.com Tokyo Access needed: 10 minutes

If the justification and search query are reasonable, nonce issues a scoped token to the AI Agent. AI Agent can only query data using a token.

If something looks fishy, i.e the AI is acting on its own, wants too much, or wants sensitive emails like bank statements, medical results, or password resets. nonce sends you a notification to approve or deny.

By default, nonce denies massive crawling behaviors

How it works 1. nonce scores each search against your original question before running it, to ensure its relevance. 2. Every search is combined with the token's search. If the AI searches "bank statement", nonce runs (from:united.com Tokyo) AND (bank statement). It can narrow its access, but not widen it. 3. The token is scoped to that agent only, with a TTL for X minutes.

title: Show HN: Doozy – an AI coworker in Slack that works in prod without your keys
author: shivsarthak
content_excerpt:
I built Doozy because support at my company (Spur) is understaffed and kept waiting on engineering to run a query for a customer, or to check whether something was a bug. The first version was a Slack bot with read access to our Postgres and Stripe, and it was very hacky. It could barely read files sent in a thread, but the agent was smart enough to find them through Slack search and finish the task anyway. It got used far more by support and success than by engineers, which surprised me. 13 people at Spur use it every day; it's basically a critical part of the team now.

Doozy is the rebuilt, multi-tenant version. You mention it in a thread with a task, it runs the task against your systems (database, Stripe, GitHub, Linear, PostHog, any MCP server, the web) in its own isolated environment, and posts the result and files in the thread.

How it touches production:

- Every job runs in a fresh sandbox (E2B today) with no credentials in it. Model calls, tool calls and git go through gateways outside the sandbox that add credentials per request. A prompt injection can make the agent misuse the tools it has, but it can't exfiltrate a key, because there isn't one to read. - Secrets the agent genuinely needs inside the sandbox (an SSH key, a CLI token) are handed over only when it asks for a named secret with a reason, and that request is logged. - Tools marked destructive start denied. Owners turn them on per tool. - Every external action writes a receipt in the thread and an append-only audit log.

title: Electrification Could Cut Global Energy Use in Half
author: jonhohle
content_excerpt:
Most people aren’t familiar with a peak demand rate because it’s not common in many markets. Take the highest kW use period of the month, and multiply kW demand by $20. Run the oven; pulls 3kW; $60. Run the oven and the stove top (1.8kW) at the same time $96. Screw up one time during the month and you might as well not care about the rest of the month.

I’m being a bit hyperbolic - it’s averaged over the highest 1 hour peak demand period (4pm-7pm, M-F), but it does limit what things can be run simultaneously (no dryer, oven and AC at the same time, for example). We schedule things around that, Our peak demand for this past month was 2.3kW. That single line item charge is higher than our entire gas bill.

There’s a separate use charge as well, but per kWh that’s pretty low. Then, of course, there’s the dozens of other random charges and fees ($86) that have nothing to do with electricity generation and everything to do with being a monopoly (court resolution surcharge: $3.58). The idea of moving more things to electric is nauseating.

title: Breaking the open web won't stop the bad bots
author: thaumasiotes
content_excerpt:
No, the definition of 'stealth bot' is a disaster. The proposed text criminalizes altering your user-agent string. It arguably criminalizes all existing user-agent strings, since their whole purpose is to lie about which browser you are.

Taking the first thing I could find, geekflare.com informs me that the current user-agent string for Google Chrome running on Windows 11 is

    Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/155.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
What's doing the work in the proposed text is the prohibition on using software "in a manner that is reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden the technical or commercial operation of" a service.

> Someone who is using a residential proxy network, headless browsing, and/or TLS fingerprint manipulation to evade rate limits and other controls to issue large volumes of automated requests under a deceptive UserAgent string isn't difficult to describe and differentiate versus a normal user using a UA.

Note that someone who's scripting a headless browser doesn't need to use a deceptive user-agent string. They can use the user-agent string for their browser, which isn't deceptive except to the degree that all user-agent strings are 90+% lies.
